If you workout with an Apple Watch on gym equipment, GymKit is absolutely worth knowing about. It's the best way for your Apple Watch to exchange workout data with machines like treadmills and ellipticals, producing results that are more accurate than either device could deliver on its own.

Apple launched GymKit back in 2017 alongside watchOS 4, but supported machines have been surprisingly hard to find. The good news is that nearly a decade later, you no longer need to spend around $15,000 on a GymKit-compatible treadmill.

You can now pick up a solid home treadmill with Apple Watch support for around $1,000. I've been testing the BowFlex T6 treadmill all summer, and it combines GymKit support, reasonable pricing, and dial-based controls to make it well worth recommending.

Why Apple GymKit is so good

GymKit provides a two-way connection between your Apple Watch and supported treadmills, ellipticals, stair climbers, and indoor bikes.

Without GymKit, cardio machines know your speed and distance but require extra hardware to measure heart rate. Your Apple Watch can track heart rate but can only estimate distance and speed on a treadmill based on your arm movement.

GymKit lets the two devices complement each other. Your Apple Watch sends heart rate data to the machine, and the machine sends back the workout data it measures directly.

Anthony Winge, Director of Product Development at Johnson Health Tech, told 9to5Mac that calories, speed, distance, pace, time, incline, and heart rate can sync in real time between the treadmill and Apple Watch, producing a more unified and accurate record in the Fitness app.

My experience with the BowFlex T6 and GymKit

The pairing process is intentionally simple, but what impressed me was how flexible the flow is. You can connect your Apple Watch before starting, but you don't have to follow a fixed order.

For example, I could start a workout on the T6's console, let the belt begin moving, and then tap my Apple Watch to the NFC sensor to confirm the connection. I didn't expect that pairing would work after the workout had already started. Starting on the treadmill first and then joining with the Apple Watch felt much more natural.

Once connected, your Apple Watch offers four GymKit workout options: Indoor Walk, Indoor Run, Time to Walk, and Time to Run. The first two are the standard Apple Watch workout experience; the latter two are for Apple Fitness+ subscribers who want to pair the treadmill's GymKit data with Apple's audio-guided workouts.

After pairing, the treadmill and Apple Watch stay connected. No matter which side you pause, resume, or end the workout on, the other side updates in sync.

During your workout, your heart rate is displayed on the treadmill's console. As Winge noted, this is especially useful for zone training, because you can monitor your heart rate without constantly looking at your wrist or gripping the machine's metal contact sensors.

BowFlex has rolled out GymKit across its existing T6, T9, and T16 treadmill lines. So you don't need to buy the most expensive model to get this feature.

iOS 27 brings GymKit to iPhone and AirPods Pro 3

Starting with iOS 27, GymKit no longer requires an Apple Watch. You can connect your iPhone to a supported machine and use AirPods Pro 3 as your heart rate source. I tried this experience with the BowFlex T6, and it's essentially the Apple Watch GymKit experience without wearing the watch.

On the other hand, watchOS 27 has improved the accuracy of wrist-movement-based estimates for indoor walking and running distance. It helps when you don't have GymKit, but connecting directly to the treadmill is still the most accurate option.

Why GymKit has always been so hard to find

The biggest issue with GymKit has always been availability.

Supported machines originally only appeared at high-end gyms in major cities. Since then, supported models have expanded to more locations in more regions, including some Planet Fitness branches, but support is still far from widespread. Even at a participating gym, only some of the machines may support GymKit.

Finding GymKit-supported equipment for a home gym has been even harder. The last time I looked in 2020, the cheapest Technogym-supported model was nearly $14,000. That's reasonable for a premium commercial setting, but out of reach for most households.

At the time, I had hoped GymKit treadmills would eventually land in the $1,000 to $1,500 range. The BowFlex T6 lands squarely in that range.

BowFlex T6 brings GymKit back home

The BowFlex T6 treadmill is priced at $999 (originally $1,299).

For a fully featured home treadmill, that's still a normal price point—roughly one-tenth of those GymKit models I looked at last time.

The T6 also avoids the expensive approach of a built-in touchscreen, opting instead for a simple, straightforward console and an adjustable device shelf so you can bring your own iPad, tablet, or phone. That lets you choose the workout platform you prefer rather than being locked into a single service.

You can use Apple Fitness+ (via Apple One Premier), Peloton, Zwift, or BowFlex's optional JRNY subscription platform. Your device connects through the T6's built-in Bluetooth speakers, while the console continues to display the workout data you need.

The treadmill itself doesn't require a subscription. In an era where many connected fitness machines charge an extra monthly fee to unlock their best features, that matters.

Dial controls are a surprisingly delightful highlight

Beyond GymKit and the approachable price, my favorite feature is how the BowFlex T6 handles speed and incline adjustments.

Instead of repeatedly tapping arrow buttons to make changes, the treadmill's handlebars are fitted with dials you can turn directly. The right dial controls speed; the left dial controls incline. Adjusting on the fly felt much faster and more natural to me.

BowFlex pairs these QuickDial controls with what it calls a MaxReact drive system, which responds very quickly when you turn the speed or incline dial. For interval training that requires frequent intensity shifts, this control scheme is especially useful.

My first time using a similar treadmill dial was a few years ago when I tried the original Peloton Tread. That machine was priced absurdly high, so seeing a similar control system on a much more affordable treadmill is a big plus.

The T6 also comes with a 20-by-60-inch cushioned running belt, a top speed of 12 mph, motor-controlled incline up to 15%, a three-speed fan, and a foldable base. For a home treadmill, these are solid fundamentals rather than padding the price with a bigger screen.

Wrap-up

Overall, I highly recommend the BowFlex T6 treadmill to anyone looking to build a home gym on a limited budget. BowFlex sells more expensive models with bigger screens and larger running decks, but the T6 covers the important features well without adding costs I wouldn't use.

GymKit with Apple Watch is a great experience, and it's recently expanded to iPhone and AirPods Pro 3. If you use a Samsung Galaxy Watch, this treadmill supports that too.

Have you tried Apple GymKit with your Apple Watch? Share your experience in the comments.
